# Addressing the longitudinal components of surgical treatments

**Authors:** Chelsea J. Messinger; Arin L. Madenci; Kerollos Nashat Wanis

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, 677 Huntington Avenue, Boston, MA 02115, USA | 2Harvard/MIT M.D.-Ph.D. Program, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Surgery, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 4Department of Surgery, Western University, London, ON, Canada

## Abstract

Despite their pre- and postoperative components, surgical treatment strategies have typically been cast as point interventions in causal inference research. When longitudinal perioperative components affect outcomes of interest, leaving them unspecified or failing to measure adherence to them complicates the interpretation of effect estimates. Inspired by two recent landmark trials that assessed the risk of stroke or death after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) compared with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), the PARTNER 3 trial and the Evolut Low Risk trial, we discuss possible ways that different postoperative therapies in treatment arms and incomplete adherence to those therapies can impact the interpretation of intention-to-treat effect estimates in surgical trials. We argue that surgical treatments are not necessarily point interventions, and make recommendations for improving the design and analysis of trials involving surgical interventions. Central to these recommendations is the need for investigators to specify and report adherence to longitudinal perioperative treatment components.

Investigators conducting randomized trials of surgical treatments often do not specify or measure adherence to pre- and postoperative intervention components when describing treatment strategies and collecting trial data. Even in contemporary discussions of trial methodology in surgery, it is commonplace to posit that, “most surgical trials consist of a single intervention” [1]. However, conceptualizing surgical treatments as single “point” interventions ignores the fact that many surgical treatment protocols include longitudinal components that affect patient outcomes. Leaving these longitudinal components unspecified or failing to measure adherence to them might result in misinterpretation of effect estimates. Even when adherence to the surgical component of the treatment strategy is perfect, and investigators are tempted to interpret intention-to-treat (ITT) effect estimates as per-protocol effects, incomplete adherence to perioperative interventions undermines this interpretation. This is true for trials comparing surgical with non-surgical treatments as well as for comparative effectiveness trials comparing different types of surgeries.

To illustrate these issues, we present an example inspired by two landmark trials published in 2019 that compared the effectiveness of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR): PARTNER 3 and the Evolut Low Risk trial [2, 3]. The primary outcome in these trials was a composite of death or stroke at 12 and 24 months, respectively (PARTNER 3 also included rehospitalization). After aortic valve replacement, anticoagulation and/or antithrombotic therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of postoperative embolic/ischemic events, with the type and duration of therapy prescribed in current practice varying according to valve type, procedure type, and patient comorbidities [4]. These postoperative therapies are therefore thought to directly affect the outcome of interest studied in the PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk trials. Although both trial protocols made recommendations for postoperative antithrombotic therapy regimens–and reportedly recorded whether patients were taking these therapies at postoperative visits–the type and duration of actual prescribed antithrombotic in each treatment arm and longitudinal adherence to these regimens were not reported in either publication. We elaborate this motivating example to argue that surgical treatments are not necessarily point interventions, and make recommendations for the design and analysis of trials involving surgical interventions.

## Hypothetical Trial Scenarios

Consider a trial comparing TAVR with SAVR for the primary outcome of death or stroke at 12 months, specifying post-implant antithrombotic therapy (12 months of either dual antiplatelet therapy [DAPT] or warfarin) as part of both treatment strategies. Suppose that adherence to antithrombotic therapy is accurately measured at postoperative visits through month 12. In Fig. 1, we present four illustrative, but not exhaustive, scenarios for antithrombotic prescription and adherence and display the relevant considerations for interpreting ITT effect estimates. Under each scenario, unique challenges may undermine the interpretation and/or transportability [5] of these estimates.

In the first scenario, treatment protocols in both arms prescribe 12 months of postoperative DAPT and patients in both arms perfectly adhere to this regimen. In this scenario, the ITT effect estimate can be interpreted as the per-protocol comparative effectiveness of the full surgical treatment protocols. However, this estimate may not be transportable or apply to clinical settings where a different antithrombotic regimen is prescribed or one where adherence to that regimen is expected to differ.

In the second scenario, treatment protocols again prescribe 12 months of postoperative DAPT in both arms. Now, however, adherence to DAPT is higher in the TAVR arm–for example, perhaps SAVR patients experience more symptoms during recovery that limit their ability to fill their prescriptions. In this setting, in addition to the transportability considerations, differences in postoperative adherence to DAPT might explain some of the difference in the effectiveness of assignment to TAVR versus assignment to SAVR, even when adherence to the surgical component is perfect.

In scenario 3, patients in the TAVR arm are prescribed 12 months of DAPT while patients in the SAVR arm are prescribed 12 months of warfarin, and both arms have the same (perfect) adherence to the prescribed regimens. Even under perfect adherence to both the surgical and postoperative components of the treatment strategy, the interpretation of the comparative effectiveness of TAVR and SAVR is complicated by the possibly differing effects of the postoperative treatment protocols. That is, differences in effectiveness cannot be attributed solely to differences in the surgical procedures. Moreover, the ITT effect estimates will again be non-transportable to clinical settings where different antithrombotic regimens are prescribed or one where adherence to those regimens differs.

Finally, in scenario 4, patients in the TAVR arm are prescribed 12 months of DAPT while patients in the SAVR arm are prescribed 12 months of warfarin, and adherence is better in the TAVR arm. Here, considerations from all the previous scenarios apply.

Each of these scenarios highlights the importance of considering longitudinal components of surgical treatment strategies in trials. In a trial where these perioperative components are not specified as part of treatment strategies, measured over time, and reported, it is impossible to distinguish which scenario the trial falls under and, therefore, how the results of that trial should be interpreted in the trial’s target population or in other populations.

## Application to PARTNER 3 and Evolut Trials

In the absence of detailed information on the postoperative antithrombotics specified by the trials, decision makers can only speculate about how longitudinal components of the surgical treatments may have impacted the results of the PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk trials. In the PARTNER 3 protocol, patients in the TAVR and the SAVR arms were recommended largely similar DAPT antithrombotic therapies. In the Evolut Low Risk protocol, patients were recommended different post-procedure antithrombotics: patients in the TAVR arm were recommended 30 days or more of DAPT followed by 12 months of aspirin, while those in the SAVR arm were recommended “a Vitamin K Antagonist (VKA) or aspirin in accordance with current guidelines.” Neither trial published more specific prescribed regimens nor reported adherence to those regimens.

The PARTNER 3 trial most closely resembles scenario 1 or 2 in Fig. 1. If patients (near) perfectly adhered to the prescribed regimen in both treatment groups, then the ITT effect estimate could be interpreted as the per-protocol effect comparing TAVR followed by 12 months of DAPT with SAVR followed by 12 months of DAPT. If adherence to DAPT differed across treatment arms, then the ITT effect estimate would not correspond to a per-protocol effect even if adherence to the surgical intervention was perfect. In either case, the effect estimate may not be applicable to clinical settings where different antithrombotic regimens are prescribed or adherence to those regimens differs. In contrast, the Evolut Low Risk trial most closely resembles scenario 3 or 4, and the comparative effectiveness of the different surgical components cannot be disentangled from the comparative effectiveness of the different postoperative regimens, even under perfect adherence to the full protocol in both arms.

The Evolut Low Risk trial reported a comparable incidence of death or disabling stroke at 24 months in the TAVR and SAVR arms (5.3% versus 6.7%, respectively), while the PARTNER 3 trial reported a lower 12-month incidence of their composite outcome in the TAVR arm compared to SAVR (8.5% versus 15.1%, respectively). While several explanations have been given for the differences in reported results for these two trials [6], we focus on the role that the postoperative treatment components might have played. Recall that the Evolut trial protocol recommended DAPT in the TAVR arm but a VKA in the SAVR arm, whereas PARTNER 3 recommended similar courses of DAPT for both arms. Compared with DAPT, warfarin has been associated with lower long-term risk of ischemic stroke and thromboembolic events as well as higher incidence of bleeding events among patients undergoing bioprosthetic SAVR [7]. If we assume that patients in both arms of the Evolut trial had similar adherence to postoperative therapies, and if VKA was in fact more effective at preventing stroke or death at 24 months compared to DAPT among trial participants, we could hypothesize that a lower incidence of the outcome was observed in the SAVR arm than might have been observed had these patients also been prescribed DAPT.

If adherence to antithrombotic regimen differed across arms in the trials, we could further hypothesize that worse adherence to antithrombotics would be associated with higher incidence of death or disabling stroke. While long-term adherence to oral antithrombotics/anticoagulation is often suboptimal for both warfarin and DAPT, warfarin has the added challenge of numerous drug/food interactions and frequent monitoring to ensure therapeutic efficacy [7, 8]. Additionally, the surgical intervention itself might impact adherence–for instance, postoperative functional status and pain is worse in patients who undergo SAVR (which requires a thoracotomy) than minimally invasive TAVR [9], which could affect patients’ ability to fill prescriptions. Thus, in both trials, it is plausible that adherence to the antithrombotic regimen differed across treatment arms, further complicating interpretation of results.

Without published information on postoperative therapy prescription and adherence in these trials, it is not possible to say whether and the extent to which these factors meaningfully impact the interpretation of the results. Moreover, while our example and exposition focused on postoperative components of the treatment strategies, similar issues arise with respect to the preoperative components of surgical interventions, for example preoperative risk assessment and optimization [10].

## Recommendations and Conclusions

We suggest three recommendations for improving the estimation of causal effects of surgical treatment strategies in randomized trials:

- Fully specify in the trial protocol all relevant components of treatment strategies that may affect the outcome, including pre- and postoperative components. If discretion is given to clinicians to choose perioperative treatments, reporting the chosen regimens would allow decision makers to better interpret trial results.

- Report longitudinal adherence to both the assigned surgical components and relevant prescribed pre- and post-operative components of the treatment protocols.

- When longitudinal perioperative components differ across treatment strategies or adherence to those components is incomplete (i.e., scenarios 2–4 in Fig. 1), perioperative components should be included in per-protocol effect estimation, if such an effect is of interest. If adherence to both surgical and longitudinal components of treatment would be expected in actual clinical practice, investigators may consider estimating the effect under hypothetical perfect adherence (the usual per-protocol effect) [11]. Alternatively, if adherence to longitudinal components would not always be expected (for example, deviations to postoperative treatment components might be allowable in the event of complications), investigators may instead consider defining dynamic treatment protocols [12] that allow for deviations from the postoperative regimen when specific events occur, and estimating corresponding per-protocol effects. In both cases, estimation of per-protocol effects would involve the use of methods (e.g., inverse probability weighting or g-computation) for time-varying confounding adjustment due to adherence-confounder feedback [13].

In sum, we argue that surgical interventions are not necessarily single “point” interventions, but are often characterized by longitudinal treatment strategies involving pre-, intra-, and postoperative treatment components. When these longitudinal components of the treatment protocol are expected to affect the outcome, addressing them head on in the trial design and analysis plan can improve the translatability and utility of results.
